where: Section 1, resolution formula vs formula box and worked example
problem: R is defined twice with different meanings. The text calls R 'the smallest printable half-pitch in nm', but the formula box and the worked example call it 'the smallest printable feature'. A student cannot tell whether R is the width of one line (the feature) or half the line-plus-space pitch.
fix: Use one definition everywhere: 'R is the smallest printable half-pitch in nm, that is, half the centre-to-centre distance of the finest line-and-space pattern the printer can resolve.'

problem: 'Both damage or blur the mask' is wrong for proximity printing. Contact printing damages the mask (and the resist). Proximity printing leaves a small gap, which blurs the printed image; the mask itself is not damaged or blurred.
fix: 'Contact printing damages the mask; proximity printing avoids the damage but the gap blurs the printed image.'

where: Quiz Q7 (and the matching line in Section 3)
problem: The answer credits epitaxy with the 'low-resistance buried collector path' and says the epi layer grows 'on the heavily doped substrate'. In BiCMOS the low-resistance path is the n+ buried layer formed in the p-substrate before growth; the epi layer itself is lightly doped and forms the collector. The substrate is lightly doped p-type, not heavily doped.
fix: Answer: 'The n+ buried layer, defined in the p-substrate before growth, gives the low-resistance collector path. The epitaxial layer grown over it is lightly doped and becomes the collector of the vertical NPN, so collector doping and thickness are set independently of the substrate.'

problem: 'About 0.5 to 0.8 for production' leaves out that production k falls well below 0.5 once resolution enhancement and immersion are used, so a student meeting advanced-node numbers will think they are wrong.
fix: 'k is a process factor, about 0.5 to 0.8 for a plain single-exposure process, and below 0.5 (down to roughly 0.25) when resolution enhancement techniques or immersion are used.'
